content.summary: Welcome to your reading mission. In this lesson, you will read short stories about everyday life, focusing on common phrasal verbs like turn on, look after, and run out of. You will learn how verbs change their meanings when combined with particles and practice spotting them in natural reading passages.

contextWarmup.prompt: When you wake up in the morning, what is the very first electronic device you turn on?
contextWarmup.explanation: Most people check their smartphones first thing in the morning to read messages or check the time.

rules: Turn on/off: verb plus particle to start or stop electronic devices. Pattern: turn on/off plus object. Example: 'Can you turn on the light?' or 'Please turn the TV off.'
Look after: care for someone or something. Pattern: look after plus object. Example: 'I look after my little brother every weekend.' This cannot be separated.
Give up: stop doing something or surrender. Pattern: give up plus doing something. Example: 'Don't give up! Keep trying.' or 'He gave up smoking last year.'
Find out: discover information or learn something. Pattern: find out plus clause. Example: 'I found out that the shop closes at 6 PM.' or 'Let me find out the answer.'
Run out of: have none left. Pattern: run out of plus noun. Example: 'We ran out of milk this morning.' or 'I am running out of time!'
Put on / Take off: wear or remove clothing items. Pattern: put on or take off plus clothing item. Example: 'Put on your jacket, it is cold.' or 'Take off your shoes before entering.'

commonTrap.explanation: Students often get confused about where to put pronouns with phrasal verbs. With separable verbs like turn on, you can put the pronoun in the middle.
commonTrap.correct: Please look after him (since look after is inseparable).

paragraphs: Emma likes to wake up early on Saturday mornings. At seven o'clock, she gets out of bed and decides to turn on the radio to listen to her favorite morning show while she drinks her coffee. After breakfast, she remembers that she needs to put on her warm jacket because the weather outside is quite cold and windy today. She checks her bag and realizes they have run out of milk, so she plans to visit the local grocery store later.

Before leaving the house, Emma remembers to turn off all the lights and the heater to save electricity. She walks down the street to pick up her friend Sarah from the train station. Afterward, they plan to look after Sarah's little puppy for the afternoon. It is a busy day, but Emma never gives up when she has many tasks to complete. She always likes to find out new ways to organize her busy weekly schedule efficiently.

connectedSpeech.note: The final consonant sound /f/ in off links directly to the vowel sound in all.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always capitalize the first letter of a sentence and proper names when using phrasal verbs.
mechanicsRules.badExample: my brother turns off the tv at night.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: My brother turns off the TV at night.
mechanicsRules.why: Sentences and proper nouns must start with capital letters.

mechanicsRules.rule: Keep verb tenses consistent when writing about daily routines and phrasal verbs.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She looks after her dog and give it water.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She looks after her dog and gives it water.
mechanicsRules.why: Subject-verb agreement must match across connected clauses.

mechanicsRules.rule: Place pronoun objects between the verb and particle for separable phrasal verbs.
mechanicsRules.why: Pronouns must sit between the verb and particle in separable phrasal verbs.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Essential Daily Phrasal Verbs in Context

content.summary: Mastering everyday phrasal verbs requires clear stress patterns, natural linking between verbs and particles, and correct intonation in daily conversations.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to where the primary stress falls in two-word verbs. Link the consonant sound at the end of the verb to the vowel sound of the particle for smooth speech.

pillars.name: Particle Stress
pillars.explanation: In most phrasal verbs, the second word or particle carries heavier vocal stress than the first verb.

pillars.name: Connected Speech
pillars.explanation: Blend words together like 'turn on' into 'turnon' when speaking at a normal conversational speed.

pillars.name: Intonation Patterns
pillars.explanation: Use falling intonation for statements using phrasal verbs and rising intonation for checking information.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the primary stress falls strongly on the second particle word.
Keep the verb short and emphasize the upward particle sound.
In three-syllable phrasal verbs, the middle syllable often carries the main stress.
Link the ending consonant of the first word directly to the vowel of the second word.
